Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Chaplain
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Event Involvement: People who are related to the event, Crowding: Crowded places, Auditory (Breathing): Heavy breathing sounds
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Vignette:
Kiet Phommasack is a thirty-four-year-old Lao-American man who works as a hospital chaplain. He was widowed three years ago when his wife died of a sudden cardiac event, and in the aftermath of that loss he had found, slowly and with considerable effort, a way to continue. His work gave him that. Moving through hospital corridors, sitting at bedsides, offering presence to people in the worst hours of their lives — it felt like the right use of whatever he had survived. Then, fourteen months ago, something happened that he has not been able to move past in the same way.

It was a Tuesday evening in late autumn. Kiet had finished a late shift and was walking to his car through the hospital's adjacent parking structure, a route he had taken hundreds of times. Two men approached him from behind a concrete pillar. One pressed close — very close — and Kiet remembers the man's breathing, laboured and damp against the side of his face, before he even understood what was happening. The other man produced a knife. They took his wallet, his phone, and the small jade pendant he wore on a cord beneath his shirt, a piece his late wife had given him. The whole encounter lasted perhaps ninety seconds. Kiet did not fight. He stood still and complied, and when they ran he sat down on the ground of the parking structure and stayed there for a long time before he could make himself move.

In the weeks that followed, the event began to assert itself in ways that felt involuntary and alien. Images returned without warning — the angle of the fluorescent light overhead, the specific grey of the concrete pillar, the face of the man who had stood closest to him. Sometimes, with no apparent prompt, Kiet would register a smell: something oily and close, the particular human warmth of a stranger's proximity, and the parking structure would be suddenly present again. When the memories arrived, what he felt was not fear but rage — a white, disorienting fury that he found deeply troubling in a man whose vocation required him to be a steady and compassionate presence. He had not told anyone about the rage.

What had settled most heavily on Kiet, however, was not the intrusions themselves but the meaning he had made of them. He had come to believe, with a quiet and persistent certainty, that the event had found him because of something intrinsic to who he was — some deficit in awareness or authority, some quality of visible softness that had marked him as a person worth targeting. He was certain that another man — someone more assured, less habitually gentle — would simply not have been in that situation. The thought that he could not prevent bad things from happening to him had taken on the texture of established fact rather than anxious speculation, and it coloured the way he moved through the world.

His daily environment had become a landscape of managed avoidance. The hospital parking structure was the first thing he changed: he now arrived early enough to use a surface lot two blocks away, adding twenty minutes to every shift. More consequentially, his work had changed. The hospital's oncology ward and its ICU were busy, often crowded corridors, and Kiet had begun routing himself around them when possible, sometimes leaving patients on his list unvisited until a colleague mentioned it. His supervisor had spoken to him twice, gently, about his reduced presence on certain floors. He had attributed it to grief fatigue, which was not entirely untrue but was not the whole story. He had also stopped attending the monthly interfaith chaplaincy gatherings he had once valued — too many people in a conference room, too much noise, too much proximity.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment three weeks ago when a porter wheeled a patient past him in a narrow corridor. The man was breathing heavily from exertion, and Kiet felt his body lock. He pressed himself against the wall and could not speak for nearly a minute. A nurse asked if he was all right. He said yes. That evening he made the referral himself.

What he fears most, sitting in the waiting room before his first session, is that the therapist will confirm what he already suspects: that this happened to him because of who he is, and that there is no changing that.
